summary: A serious fungal disease of grapes. Leaf spots are a warning sign; berry infections can destroy most of the crop.
symptoms: Reddish-brown circular leaf spots with a dark border
Tiny black dots (fruiting bodies) inside the spots
Berries turn brown, then shrivel into hard black mummies
key_sign: Round reddish-brown spots with tiny black dots in a ring near the edge.
favourable_conditions: Warm, wet weather; infection needs the leaves to stay wet for several hours.
spread: Overwinters in mummified berries and cane lesions; spores spread by rain splash and wind.

today: Remove mummified berries from the vines and the ground
this_week: Apply a fungicide registered for grape black rot, especially from early shoot growth until berries begin to colour
Open the canopy (shoot positioning, leaf removal) so leaves dry faster
next_two_weeks: Repeat protection at label intervals during wet weather
Inspect clusters; berries are most susceptible from bloom to about four weeks after

chemical: Protectants such as mancozeb or captan, and systemic DMI or QoI fungicides labelled for black rot; rotate groups
organic: Copper and sulfur give only partial control; sanitation is critical in organic vineyards
cultural: Remove mummies and infected canes during dormant pruning

prevention: Choose less susceptible varieties where possible
Keep a clean vineyard floor and an open canopy

pathogen: Phaeomoniella chlamydospora, Phaeoacremonium spp. and other wood-infecting fungi
summary: A trunk disease: fungi infect pruning wounds and live permanently inside the wood. Leaf 'tiger stripes' appear each year and vines decline.
symptoms: Interveinal yellow or red stripes that dry to brown ('tiger stripes')
Small dark spots on berries (black measles)
Sudden collapse of a whole shoot or vine in hot weather (apoplexy)
Dark streaks in the wood when the trunk is cut
key_sign: Tiger-stripe pattern between the veins with dry brown centres.
favourable_conditions: Infection happens through pruning wounds, especially during rainy weather in the dormant season.
spread: Spores enter fresh pruning wounds; once inside the wood, the infection cannot be cured by sprays.

today: Flag symptomatic vines so you can track them each season
Do not use cuttings from these vines for propagation
this_week: Contact your agriculture officer or a viticulture specialist to confirm (lab tests may be needed)
Plan remedial surgery: cut the trunk well below the dark-stained wood and retrain a new trunk
next_two_weeks: Remove and burn badly infected wood; never leave it in the vineyard

chemical: No fungicide cures existing infections. Registered pruning-wound protectants can reduce new infections
organic: Wound sealants or biological wound protectants (such as Trichoderma-based products) applied right after pruning
cultural: Prune in dry weather, late in the dormant season
Use double pruning: pre-prune long, then make final cuts close to bud break

summary: A fungal leaf spot that appears later in the season, mainly in warm, humid regions, and can cause early leaf drop.
symptoms: Irregular dark brown to black spots on older leaves, often with a yellow edge
Spots merge into large dead patches
Early leaf drop in severe cases
key_sign: Irregular dark brown patches on older leaves without the ring of black dots seen in black rot.
favourable_conditions: Warm, humid weather late in the season, especially in dense canopies.
spread: Spreads from infected leaves by rain splash and wind; survives on fallen leaves.

today: Remove heavily spotted leaves from the lower canopy
this_week: Improve airflow by thinning shoots and leaves around clusters
If spread continues, apply a fungicide registered for grape leaf spots
next_two_weeks: Monitor older leaves; keep the vineyard floor clean

chemical: Mancozeb, copper oxychloride or other fungicides labelled for grape leaf spots

prevention: Balanced fertilisation to avoid dense, soft growth

key_sign: Uniform green leaf with no spots.

this_week: Inspect a few plants, including leaf undersides
next_two_weeks: Keep monitoring, especially after rain or humid spells

cultural: Keep an open canopy with good airflow

prevention: Keep an open canopy with good airflow
Protect pruning wounds in wet weather
